proof_tex:
Fix \(a\in\mathcal A\). For every Borel set \(B\subseteq\mathcal Y\), conditional ignorability, consistency, and fixed overlap give, for \(P_{X,n}\)-almost every \(x\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mu_{a,P_n}(B\mid x)
&=P_n\{Y_n(a)\in B\mid X_n=x\}\\
&=P_n\{Y_n(a)\in B\mid A_n=a,X_n=x\}\\
&=P_n\{Y_n\in B\mid A_n=a,X_n=x\}\\
&=Q_{a,P_n}(B\mid x).
\end{aligned}
\]
The second equality uses \(\texttt{ass:ignorability}\), the third uses \(\texttt{ass:consistency}\), and \(\texttt{ass:fixed-overlap}\) ensures that the arm conditional law is defined. Applying \(\texttt{lem:conditional-coupling-sharpness}\) to these two conditional marginals proves that \(\theta_n\) is the sharp conditional-coupling lower endpoint of \(E[\lVert Y_n(1)-Y_n(0)\rVert_2^2]\), while keeping the causal target distinct from its observed-law representation.

It remains to calculate the observed-data canonical gradient. Fix \(P_n\in\mathcal M_n^{\mathrm{reg}}\) satisfying \(\texttt{ass:regular-support-geometry}\), and let \(t\mapsto P_{n,t}\) be an arbitrary regular dominated submodel through \(P_n\), with score \(h\in L_0^2(P_n)\). Write
\[
h_X(x)=E[h(O)\mid X=x],\qquad h_{Y,a}(x,y)=h(x,a,y)-E[h(O)\mid A=a,X=x].
\]
By \(\texttt{lem:integrated-arm-path-differentiation}\),
\[
\dot\theta_n(h)=E[(V_n(X_n)-\theta_n)h_X(X_n)]+\sum_aE_{P_{X,n}}\!\left[\int\phi_{a,n}(X_n,y)h_{Y,a}(X_n,y)Q_{a,P_n}(dy\mid X_n)\right].
\]
The first term equals \(E[(V_n(X_n)-\theta_n)h(O)]\), because \(V_n(X_n)-\theta_n\) is \(X_n\)-measurable. For an arm term, iterated expectation and overlap give
\[
\begin{aligned}
&E\!\left[\frac{1\{A_n=a\}}{\pi_{a,n}(X_n)}\phi_{a,n}(X_n,Y_n)h(O)\right]\\
&\quad=E_{P_{X,n}}\!\left[\int\phi_{a,n}(X_n,y)h(X_n,a,y)Q_{a,P_n}(dy\mid X_n)\right]\\
&\quad=E_{P_{X,n}}\!\left[\int\phi_{a,n}(X_n,y)h_{Y,a}(X_n,y)Q_{a,P_n}(dy\mid X_n)\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
The last equality uses the exact centering \(\int\phi_{a,n}(x,y)Q_{a,P_n}(dy\mid x)=0\), which removes \(E[h\mid A=a,X=x]\). Consequently, for every regular score \(h\),
\[
\dot\theta_n(h)=E_{P_n}[\psi_n(O)h(O)].
\]
By \(\texttt{lem:uniform-canonical-gradient-bound}\), \(\psi_n\) is mean zero and bounded, hence belongs to \(L_0^2(P_n)\). The tangent-space closure of the dominated nonparametric observed-data model is \(L_0^2(P_n)\): bounded mean-zero functions are scores of bounded tilting submodels and are dense in \(L_0^2(P_n)\). Thus the preceding identity identifies \(\psi_n\) as the unique Riesz representer of the pathwise derivative, namely the canonical gradient. Its squared \(L^2(P_n)\)-norm is therefore the semiparametric efficiency bound, namely
\[
E_{P_n}[\psi_n(O)^2]=\sigma_n^2.
\]
This proves all assertions.

Let
\[a_\pi=\frac{t_\pi}{2t_\pi+d_X},\qquad a_q=\frac{s}{2s+D}.\]
By \(\texttt{lem:finite-net-propensity-rate}\), the primitive learner satisfies the generic uniform condition in \(\texttt{def:propensity-rate-regimes}\) with \(r_{\pi,n}=n^{-a_\pi}\). By \(\texttt{def:foldwise-rate-route}\), \(r_{q,n}=n^{-a_q}\). Since \(t_\pi,s>0\), both rates tend to zero, so \(r_{\pi,n}+r_{q,n}=o(1)\). Moreover,
\[r_{q,n}^2=o(n^{-1/2})\Longleftrightarrow 2a_q>\frac12\Longleftrightarrow s>\frac D2,\]
and
\[r_{\pi,n}r_{q,n}=o(n^{-1/2})\Longleftrightarrow a_\pi+a_q>\frac12.\]
Thus the two displayed restrictions imply all three rate hypotheses of \(\texttt{thm:regular-efficient-inference}\). Since all denominators are positive,
\[\begin{aligned}&\frac{t_\pi}{2t_\pi+d_X}+\frac{s}{2s+D}>\frac12\\&\quad\Longleftrightarrow 2t_\pi(2s+D)+2s(2t_\pi+d_X)>(2t_\pi+d_X)(2s+D)\\&\quad\Longleftrightarrow4st_\pi>Dd_X\Longleftrightarrow t_\pi>\frac{Dd_X}{4s}.\end{aligned}\]
If the propensity is known, \(\bar\pi_{-k,n}=\pi_n\) makes the propensity error and product remainder identically zero, leaving only \(s>D/2\). If a predetermined correctly specified fixed-dimensional learner satisfies \(r_{\pi,n}=n^{-1/2}\), then
\[r_{\pi,n}r_{q,n}=n^{-1/2}r_{q,n}=o(n^{-1/2}),\qquad r_{\pi,n}+r_{q,n}=o(1),\]
because \(r_{q,n}\to0\); again only \(s>D/2\) remains.

The conditional-transport conclusions of \(\texttt{lem:conditional-transport-stability-rates}\), followed by \(\texttt{lem:assignment-score-rates}\), verify the hypotheses of \(\texttt{lem:cross-fit-remainder-variance}\). That lemma gives the exact fold-bias identity in the statement. Its signed transport term is nonpositive and has order \(O_{P_n}(r_{q,n}^2)\), while its propensity correction has order \(O_{P_n}(r_{\pi,n}r_{q,n})\), uniformly over \(\mathbf P\in\mathscr C\).

Since \(r_{S,n}=r_{\pi,n}+2r_{q,n}\), the same lemma gives
\[
\widehat\theta_n-\theta_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_n(O_{i,n})+R_n
\]
with
\[
R_n=O_{P_n}\!\left(r_{q,n}^2+r_{\pi,n}r_{q,n}+n^{-1/2}(r_{\pi,n}+2r_{q,n})\right).
\]
The first two rate hypotheses make the first two terms \(o(n^{-1/2})\), and the third hypothesis implies \(r_{\pi,n}+2r_{q,n}=o(1)\). Hence \(R_n=o_{P_n}(n^{-1/2})\) uniformly over \(\mathscr C\). The variance conclusion of the same lemma and \(r_{\sigma,n}=r_{S,n}+n^{-1/2}\) give
\[
\widehat\sigma_n^2-\sigma_n^2=O_{P_n}(r_{\pi,n}+2r_{q,n}+n^{-1/2})=o_{P_n}(1).
\]
By \(\texttt{lem:uniform-canonical-gradient-bound}\), \(P_n\psi_n=0\) and \(\psi_n\) has a common finite almost-sure envelope. The class definition supplies \(\sigma_n\ge\sigma_\star>0\), and the observations are i.i.d. within each row. All hypotheses of \(\texttt{lem:uniform-studentized-limit}\) are therefore satisfied. It follows that
\[
\sup_{\mathbf P\in\mathscr C}\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}\left|P_n\!\left(\frac{\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_n)}{\widehat\sigma_n}\le t\right)-\Phi(t)\right|\longrightarrow0.
\]
That lemma also yields \(\widehat\sigma_n/\sigma_n\to1\) uniformly in probability and
\[
\inf_{\mathbf P\in\mathscr C}P_n(\widehat\sigma_n>0)\longrightarrow1.
\]
For \(z=z_{1-\alpha/2}\), on \(\{\widehat\sigma_n>0\}\),
\[
\left\{\theta_n\in\left[\widehat\theta_n-z\widehat\sigma_n/\sqrt n,\widehat\theta_n+z\widehat\sigma_n/\sqrt n\right]\right\}=\left\{\left|\frac{\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_n)}{\widehat\sigma_n}\right|\le z\right\}.
\]
Uniform convergence at \(-z\) and \(z\), continuity of \(\Phi\), and the uniformly negligible zero-denominator event prove uniform asymptotic coverage \(1-\alpha\). Finally, \(\texttt{thm:observed-gradient}\) identifies \(\psi_n\) as the observed-data canonical gradient and \(\sigma_n^2=P_n\psi_n^2\) as the semiparametric efficiency bound. The displayed asymptotic linear representation has influence function \(\psi_n\); consequently the estimator's leading variance attains that bound.

Fix a fold and arm, put \(m=n-|I_{k,n}|\asymp n\), and condition on the full treatment-label vector in the training sample. If \(N=N_{a,-k,n}\), the selected observations are independent with common law \(P_n(\cdot\mid A_n=a)\). Since \(P_n(A_n=a)\ge\varepsilon\), a binomial exponential-moment bound gives, uniformly in \(\mathbf P\in\mathscr P\),
\[P_n(N<\varepsilon m/2)\le e^{-c_0m}\]
for a common \(c_0>0\). This also dispatches the exceptional rule used when \(N=0\).

Suppress indices and define
\[\ell_f(x,y)=\int_{\mathcal Y}f(x,z)^2d\ell_{\mathcal Y}(z)-2f(x,y),\qquad \mathcal R(f)=E[\ell_f-ell_q\mid A=a].\]
Expansion followed by conditioning on \(X\) gives
\[\mathcal R(f)=\lVert f-q\rVert_{L^2(P_{X\mid A=a}\otimes\ell_{\mathcal Y})}^2.\]
Because \(f,q\in[c,C]\) on compact support, there is a common \(B<\infty\) such that \(|\ell_f-ell_q|\le B\) and
\[\operatorname{Var}(\ell_f-ell_q\mid A=a)\le B\mathcal R(f).\]
Indeed, conditional Cauchy--Schwarz controls the difference of the integrated squares, while \(E[(f-q)^2(X,Y)\mid X,A=a]\le C\int(f-q)^2(X,y)d\ell_{\mathcal Y}(y)\). For a centered \(Z\) with \(|Z|\le B\) and \(E[Z^2]=v\), the exponential series and \(E|Z|^r\le B^{r-2}v\) give
\[\log E(e^{tZ})\le\frac{t^2v}{2(1-|t|B/3)},\qquad |t|<3/B.\]
Exponential Markov optimization and a union bound over the net imply that, with probability at least \(1-2e^{-u}\), simultaneously for every candidate,
\[|({\mathbb P}_N-P)(\ell_f-\ell_q)|\le\frac14\mathcal R(f)+C_1\frac{\log|\mathfrak F_{J_n}|+u}{N}.\]

To justify the feasible net, truncate the tensor-wavelet expansion at level \(J\), partition its coefficient space into cells using level-dependent meshes whose level-\(j\) contribution to sup-norm error is \(2^{-Js}2^{-\kappa(J-j)}\), retain only cells intersecting \(\mathfrak F\), and choose one predetermined representative from each nonempty intersection. Every representative therefore satisfies normalization and the box constraints exactly. The H\"older coefficient envelope and summation over levels give cover radius \(C2^{-Js}\) and
\[\log|\mathfrak F_J|\le C\sum_{j\le J}2^{jD}(J-j+1)\le C'2^{JD}.\]
Thus some \(f^\circ\in\mathfrak F_{J_n}\) satisfies \(\lVert f^\circ-q\rVert_\infty\le C_2 2^{-J_ns}\). The empirical minimizing property, used with the preceding deviation inequality for \(\widehat q\) and \(f^\circ\), yields
\[\mathcal R(\widehat q)\le C_3\left\{2^{-2J_ns}+\frac{\log|\mathfrak F_{J_n}|+u}{N}\right\}.\]
On the high-probability count event the second term is \(O((2^{J_nD}+u)/n)\). Overlap gives
\[\varepsilon\lVert f-q\rVert_{L^2(P_X\otimes\ell_{\mathcal Y})}^2\le\lVert f-q\rVert_{L^2(P_{X\mid A=a}\otimes\ell_{\mathcal Y})}^2\le\varepsilon^{-1}\lVert f-q\rVert_{L^2(P_X\otimes\ell_{\mathcal Y})}^2.\]
Taking square roots and a union bound over the fixed \(2K\) fold-arm pairs proves the first asserted uniform order. Finally \(2^{J_nD}\asymp n^{D/(2s+D)}\) balances the two terms and gives \(n^{-s/(2s+D)}\).

Fix a fold \(k\) and suppress \(k,n\) from the notation. For \(a\in\mathcal A\), put
\[
e_a(x,y)=\widehat q_a(x,y)-q_a(x,y),\qquad d_a(x)=W_2\!\left(\widehat Q_a(\cdot\mid x),Q_a(\cdot\mid x)\right).
\]
Both conditional densities are bounded below by \(c\). Hence \(\texttt{lem:wasserstein-l2-density-control}\), applied for almost every \(x\), gives
\[
d_a(x)^2\le c^{-1}C_{\mathcal Y}^2\int_{\mathcal Y}e_a(x,y)^2d\ell_{\mathcal Y}(y).
\]
After integration with respect to \(P_{X,n}\), \(\texttt{lem:finite-net-conditional-density-rate}\) yields
\[
\max_{k,a}\int d_{a,k,n}(x)^2dP_{X,n}(x)=O_{P_n}(r_{q,n}^2)
\]
uniformly over \(\mathbf P\in\mathscr P^{\mathrm{vu}}\).

We next compare the dual potentials. At a fixed \(x\) in the common full-measure set supplied by the three conditional Brenier assumptions, write \(h_a=\widehat u_a-u_a\), with arbitrary additive constants. Apply \(\texttt{lem:two-sample-map-stability}\) to the forward true and fitted maps and then to the reverse maps. The identities between gradients of quadratic Kantorovich potentials and the corresponding Brenier maps, together with \(c\le q_a,\widehat q_a\le C\), imply
\[
\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}\lVert\nabla_yh_a(x,\cdot)\rVert_{L^2(\ell_{\mathcal Y})}^2\le C_1\{d_0(x)+d_1(x)\}^2. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, the forward inequality controls the map difference under \(\widehat Q_0\), the reverse inequality controls the reverse-map difference under \(\widehat Q_1\), and the common density lower bound converts those controls to \(L^2(\ell_{\mathcal Y})\) bounds. The argument is invariant to additive normalization.

Let \(Q_ah_a=\int h_a\,dQ_a\). Exact centering gives
\[
\widehat\phi_a-\phi_a=h_a-Q_ah_a+(Q_a-\widehat Q_a)\widehat u_a. \tag{2}
\]
The weighted Poincar\'e inequality, obtained from the ordinary Poincar\'e inequality and \(c\le q_a\le C\), gives
\[
\lVert h_a-Q_ah_a\rVert_{L^2(Q_a)}\le C_2\lVert\nabla_yh_a\rVert_{L^2(\ell_{\mathcal Y})}. \tag{3}
\]
An additive constant in \(\widehat u_a\) integrates to zero against \(Q_a-\widehat Q_a\). Quadratic dual conjugacy on compact \(\mathcal Y\) gives a common oscillation bound for \(\widehat u_a\); hence
\[
|(Q_a-\widehat Q_a)\widehat u_a|\le C_3\lVert e_a(x,\cdot)\rVert_{L^1(\ell_{\mathcal Y})}\le C_4\lVert e_a(x,\cdot)\rVert_{L^2(\ell_{\mathcal Y})}. \tag{4}
\]
Combining (1)--(4), squaring, and integrating in \(x\) gives
\[
\max_{k,a}\lVert\widehat\phi_{a,-k,n}-\phi_{a,n}\rVert_{L^2(\nu_{a,n})}^2=O_{P_n}(r_{q,n}^2).
\]
Taking square roots proves the potential rate.

Let \(w(x)=W_2(Q_0(\cdot\mid x),Q_1(\cdot\mid x))\) and let \(\widehat w(x)\) be its fitted analogue. The triangle inequality gives \(|\widehat w-w|\le d_0+d_1\). Since both distances are bounded by \(\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal Y)\),
\[
|\widehat V(x)-V(x)|\le2\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal Y)\{d_0(x)+d_1(x)\}.
\]
The first conclusion therefore implies \(\max_k\lVert\widehat V_{-k,n}-V_n\rVert_{L^2(P_{X,n})}=O_{P_n}(r_{q,n})\).

Finally apply \(\texttt{lem:two-sample-quadratic-remainder}\), conditionally at \(x\), with the fitted pair as base and the true pair as perturbation. Centering the fitted potentials does not change the linear term. Thus
\[
\widehat V_{-k,n}-V_n+\sum_a\int\widehat\phi_{a,-k,n}\,d(Q_{a,P_n}-\widehat Q_{a,-k,n})=-\mathscr D_{\mathrm{OT}}(Q,\widehat Q)\le0.
\]
Moreover,
\[
E_{P_{X,n}}\mathscr D_{\mathrm{OT}}(Q,\widehat Q)\le C_{\mathrm{OT}}E_{P_{X,n}}\{d_0(X_n)+d_1(X_n)\}^2=O_{P_n}(r_{q,n}^2).
\]
Thus the asserted absolute order is the \(L^1(P_{X,n})\) order needed downstream. All bounds are uniform over the fixed finite set of fold--arm pairs and over \(\mathbf P\in\mathscr P^{\mathrm{vu}}\).

Since the remainder is the nonpositive function \(-\mathscr D_{\mathrm{OT}}(Q,\widehat Q)\), the last display also gives the explicitly typed conclusion
\[
\max_k\left\|\widehat V_{-k,n}-V_n+\sum_a\int\widehat\phi_{a,-k,n}\,d(Q_{a,P_n}-\widehat Q_{a,-k,n})\right\|_{L^1(P_{X,n})}
=\max_kE_{P_{X,n}}\mathscr D_{\mathrm{OT}}(Q,\widehat Q)
=O_{P_n}(r_{q,n}^2).
\]

Put \(h=g-f\), so \(\int_{\mathcal Y}h\,d\ell_{\mathcal Y}=0\). On the mean-zero subspace of \(H^1(\mathcal Y)\), the Poincar\'e inequality makes
\[
\eta\longmapsto\frac12\int_{\mathcal Y}\lVert\nabla\eta\rVert_2^2d\ell_{\mathcal Y}-\int_{\mathcal Y}h\eta\,d\ell_{\mathcal Y}
\]
coercive and strictly convex. Its minimizer \(\varphi\), normalized to have mean zero, satisfies
\[
\int_{\mathcal Y}\nabla\varphi\cdot\nabla\eta\,d\ell_{\mathcal Y}=\int_{\mathcal Y}h\eta\,d\ell_{\mathcal Y},\qquad \lVert\nabla\varphi\rVert_2\le C_{\mathcal Y}\lVert h\rVert_2.
\]
Set \(\rho_t=(1-t)f+tg\), \(j_t=\nabla\varphi\), and \(v_t=j_t/\rho_t\). Then \(\rho_t\ge c\), the weak identity gives \(\partial_t\rho_t+\nabla\cdot j_t=0\) with zero normal flux, and
\[
\int_0^1\!\int_{\mathcal Y}\rho_t\lVert v_t\rVert_2^2d\ell_{\mathcal Y}dt\le c^{-1}C_{\mathcal Y}^2\lVert f-g\rVert_2^2. \tag{1}
\]
To pass from this weak path to a coupling, regularize the continuity equation on the bounded Lipschitz domain, preserving mass, the zero-flux boundary condition, and the lower bound \(c\). For each regularized path the characteristic flow supplies a coupling of its endpoints. Along every characteristic, Cauchy--Schwarz gives its squared endpoint displacement no larger than its time-integrated kinetic energy; integration over starting points bounds the resulting coupling cost by the regularized version of (1). The regularizations converge to \(f\) and \(g\) in \(L^1\). Because \(\mathcal Y\) is compact, this endpoint convergence also holds in \(W_2\), and lower semicontinuity of the optimal transport cost permits passage to the limit. Consequently,
\[
W_2^2(f\,d\ell_{\mathcal Y},g\,d\ell_{\mathcal Y})\le c^{-1}C_{\mathcal Y}^2\lVert f-g\rVert_{L^2(\ell_{\mathcal Y})}^2,
\]
as claimed.

Write \(F(P)=W_2^2(P_0,P_1)\) and \(d_a=W_2(P_a,\overline P_a)\), and let \((u_0,u_1)\) optimize the perturbed pair. Feasibility of the base optimizer at the perturbed pair gives
\[F(P)\ge F(\overline P)+\sum_a\int\overline u_a\,d(P_a-\overline P_a),\]
so \(\mathscr D_{\mathrm{OT}}(P,\overline P)\ge0\). Feasibility of the perturbed optimizer at the base pair likewise gives
\[\mathscr D_{\mathrm{OT}}(P,\overline P)\le\sum_a\int(u_a-\overline u_a)\,d(P_a-\overline P_a).\]
The forward and reverse inequalities in \(\texttt{lem:two-sample-map-stability}\), the identities between gradients of quadratic dual potentials and the corresponding maps, and the common density bounds imply
\[\sum_a\lVert\nabla(u_a-\overline u_a)\rVert_{L^2(\ell_{\mathcal Y})}^2\le C(d_0+d_1)^2.\]
For each arm take an optimal coupling of \(\overline P_a\) and \(P_a\) and its displacement interpolation. Convexity of \(\mathcal Y\) keeps every segment inside the support. If \(\rho_t\) is the interpolating density, the displacement-convexity inequality
\[\rho_t^{-1/d_Y}\ge(1-t)\rho_0^{-1/d_Y}+t\rho_1^{-1/d_Y}\]
along transport rays and the common endpoint upper bound give \(\rho_t\le C\). The fundamental theorem of calculus along the rays and Cauchy--Schwarz therefore yield, for every \(v\in H^1(\mathcal Y)\),
\[\left|\int v\,d(P_a-\overline P_a)\right|\le C^{1/2}d_a\lVert\nabla v\rVert_{L^2(\ell_{\mathcal Y})}.\]
Taking \(v=u_a-\overline u_a\), summing, and using the gradient bound proves
\[\mathscr D_{\mathrm{OT}}(P,\overline P)\le C_{\mathrm{OT}}(d_0+d_1)^2.\]
Centering only adds constants, whose integrals against \(P_a-\overline P_a\) vanish.

Use the half-squared semi-dual
\[S_{\widehat P,\widehat Q}(b)=\int b\,d\widehat P+\int b^*\,d\widehat Q,\qquad \Delta=S_{\widehat P,\widehat Q}(b)-\min_{\widetilde b}S_{\widehat P,\widehat Q}(\widetilde b).\]
The curvature assumptions give \(m_{\mathrm{OT}}I\preceq\nabla^2b\preceq M_{\mathrm{OT}}I\). Thus \(b^*\) is \(M_{\mathrm{OT}}^{-1}\)-strongly convex and \(m_{\mathrm{OT}}^{-1}\)-smooth. If \(\widehat\gamma\) is optimal, Fenchel equality for its optimizer and \(T=\nabla b\) imply
\[\Delta=\int\{b(\xi)+b^*(\zeta)-\langle\xi,\zeta\rangle\}d\widehat\gamma\ge\frac1{2M_{\mathrm{OT}}}\int\lVert\zeta-T(\xi)\rVert_2^2d\widehat\gamma.\]
For the upper bound, draw \(X\sim P\), set \(Y=T(X)\), couple \(X\) optimally to \(U\sim\widehat P\), and, independently given \((X,Y)\), couple \(Y\) optimally to \(V\sim\widehat Q\). The induced law \(\eta\) of \((U,V)\) couples \(\widehat P\) and \(\widehat Q\). Quadratic transport maximizes \(E\langle U,V\rangle\), so
\[\Delta\le S_{\widehat P,\widehat Q}(b)-E_\eta\langle U,V\rangle.\]
Expansion about \((X,Y)\), using \(Y=\nabla b(X)\), gives
\[b(U)+b^*(V)-\langle U,V\rangle\le\frac{M_{\mathrm{OT}}}{2}\lVert U-X\rVert_2^2+\frac1{2m_{\mathrm{OT}}}\lVert V-Y\rVert_2^2-\langle U-X,V-Y\rangle.\]
Cauchy--Schwarz and optimality of the endpoint couplings yield
\[\Delta\le\frac{M_{\mathrm{OT}}}{2}W_2^2(P,\widehat P)+\frac1{2m_{\mathrm{OT}}}W_2^2(Q,\widehat Q)+W_2(P,\widehat P)W_2(Q,\widehat Q).\]
Combining the bounds and multiplying by two proves the assertion. Applying the same argument to the conjugate potential after swapping the marginals proves the reverse-map version.

Fix a fold \(k\) and suppress row and fold indices. Put
\[
g_a(x)=\int\widehat\phi_a(x,y)d(Q_a-\widehat Q_a)(y\mid x).
\]
Exact centering under the fitted kernel and centering of the true potential give
\[
g_a(x)=\int(\widehat\phi_a-\phi_a)(x,y)Q_a(dy\mid x).
\]
Jensen's inequality and the potential conclusion of \(\texttt{lem:conditional-transport-stability-rates}\) imply
\[
\lVert g_a\rVert_{L^2(P_X)}\le\lVert\widehat\phi_a-\phi_a\rVert_{L^2(\nu_a)}=O_{P_n}(r_{q,n}).
\]
Fixed overlap and clipping yield
\[
\left|\frac{\pi_a}{\bar\pi_a}-1\right|\le\varepsilon^{-1}|\pi_a-\bar\pi_a|.
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz in \(P_X\), the generic propensity rate, and the preceding display therefore give
\[
\left|E_{P_X}\sum_a\left(\frac{\pi_a}{\bar\pi_a}-1\right)g_a\right|=O_{P_n}(r_{\pi,n}r_{q,n}).
\]
Taking the maximum over fixed \(K\) preserves the order and proves the first assertion.

For the score bound, write \(S^\circ=\theta+\psi\). Since exactly one arm indicator is nonzero,
\[
\widehat S-S^\circ=(\widehat V-V)+\sum_a1\{A=a\}\left\{\frac{\widehat\phi_a-\phi_a}{\bar\pi_a}+\phi_a\left(\frac1{\bar\pi_a}-\frac1{\pi_a}\right)\right\}.
\]
The compact quadratic cost and conjugacy give \(|\phi_a|\le2\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal Y)^2\), as in \(\texttt{lem:uniform-canonical-gradient-bound}\). Fixed overlap and clipping imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
\lVert\widehat S-S^\circ\rVert_{L^2(P)}
&\le\lVert\widehat V-V\rVert_{L^2(P_X)}+\varepsilon^{-1}\sum_a\lVert\widehat\phi_a-\phi_a\rVert_{L^2(\nu_a)}\\
&\quad+C\sum_a\lVert\bar\pi_a-\pi_a\rVert_{L^2(P_X)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The transport-only value and potential rates make the first two contributions \(O_{P_n}(r_{q,n})\), and the generic learner condition makes the last \(O_{P_n}(r_{\pi,n})\). Hence
\[
\max_k\lVert\widehat S_{-k,n}-(\theta_n+\psi_n)\rVert_{L^2(P_n)}=O_{P_n}(r_{\pi,n}+2r_{q,n}),
\]
uniformly over \(\mathbf P\in\mathscr C\).

Let \(R=\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal Y)\). The quadratic cost lies in \([0,R^2]\), so \(0\le V_n(x),\theta_n\le R^2\) and \(|V_n(x)-\theta_n|\le R^2\). For \(y,y',z\in\mathcal Y\),
\[
|\lVert y-z\rVert_2^2-\lVert y'-z\rVert_2^2|\le2R\lVert y-y'\rVert_2\le2R^2.
\]
Taking the relevant infimum or supremum in the conjugacy formula preserves this oscillation bound, so \(\operatorname{osc}(u_{a,n}(x,\cdot))\le2R^2\). Centering implies \(|\phi_{a,n}(x,y)|\le2R^2\). Exactly one arm indicator is nonzero and overlap gives \(\pi_{a,n}(X_n)\ge\varepsilon\); therefore
\[
|\psi_n(O)|\le R^2+\frac{2R^2}{\varepsilon}=:M_\psi.
\]
Exact centering gives
\[
E\!\left[\frac{1\{A_n=a\}}{\pi_{a,n}(X_n)}\phi_{a,n}(X_n,Y_n)\,\middle|\,X_n\right]=\int\phi_{a,n}(X_n,y)Q_{a,P_n}(dy\mid X_n)=0,
\]
and \(E[V_n(X_n)-\theta_n]=0\). Thus \(E[\psi_n]=0\). Finally, the almost-sure envelope gives \(E|\psi_n|^r\le M_\psi^r\) for every \(r\ge1\), uniformly in \(n\) and in every law under consideration.

Put \(m_{k,n}=|I_{k,n}|\), \(w_{k,n}=m_{k,n}/n\), and let \(\mathbb P_{k,n}\) denote the empirical measure on fold \(I_{k,n}\). Define
\[
\delta_{k,n}(o)=\widehat S_{-k,n}(o)-\{\theta_n+\psi_n(o)\}.
\]
Conditional on \(\mathcal T_{-k,n}\), this is a fixed measurable function and the observations in \(I_{k,n}\) are independent with law \(P_n\).

Conditioning successively on \(X_n\) and \(A_n\) gives
\[
P_n\widehat S_{-k,n}=E_{P_{X,n}}\!\left[\widehat V_{-k,n}+\sum_a\frac{\pi_{a,n}}{\bar\pi_{a,-k,n}}\int\widehat\phi_{a,-k,n}\,dQ_{a,P_n}\right].
\]
Because \(\int\widehat\phi_{a,-k,n}d\widehat Q_{a,-k,n}=0\), adding and subtracting the fitted kernel and writing \(\pi_a/\bar\pi_a=1+(\pi_a/\bar\pi_a-1)\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_n\widehat S_{-k,n}-\theta_n
={}&E_{P_{X,n}}\!\left[\widehat V_{-k,n}-V_n+\sum_a\int\widehat\phi_{a,-k,n}d(Q_{a,P_n}-\widehat Q_{a,-k,n})\right]\\
&+E_{P_{X,n}}\sum_a\left(\frac{\pi_{a,n}}{\bar\pi_{a,-k,n}}-1\right)\int\widehat\phi_{a,-k,n}d(Q_{a,P_n}-\widehat Q_{a,-k,n}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(P_n\psi_n=0\), the left side is \(P_n\delta_{k,n}=\mathcal B_{k,n}\). The final identity in \(\texttt{lem:conditional-transport-stability-rates}\) proves the exact fold-bias formula. Its first term is nonpositive and \(O_{P_n}(r_{q,n}^2)\), while \(\texttt{lem:assignment-score-rates}\) gives \(O_{P_n}(r_{\pi,n}r_{q,n})\) for the second.

The estimator has the exact decomposition
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat\theta_n-\theta_n
&=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_n(O_{i,n})+\sum_k w_{k,n}\mathbb P_{k,n}\delta_{k,n}\\
&=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_n(O_{i,n})+\sum_k w_{k,n}\mathcal B_{k,n}+\sum_k w_{k,n}(\mathbb P_{k,n}-P_n)\delta_{k,n}.
\end{aligned} \tag{1}
\]
Conditionally on the training sample,
\[
E\!\left[\{(\mathbb P_{k,n}-P_n)\delta_{k,n}\}^2\,\middle|\,\mathcal T_{-k,n}\right]\le\frac{P_n\delta_{k,n}^2}{m_{k,n}}.
\]
By \(\texttt{lem:assignment-score-rates}\), \(\max_k\lVert\delta_{k,n}\rVert_{L^2(P_n)}=O_{P_n}(r_{S,n})\). Balanced folds, fixed \(K\), and conditional Chebyshev therefore give
\[
\sum_k w_{k,n}(\mathbb P_{k,n}-P_n)\delta_{k,n}=O_{P_n}(n^{-1/2}r_{S,n}) \tag{2}
\]
uniformly. Combining (1), (2), and the bias orders proves the estimator expansion.

For the studentizer, put \(e_n=\widehat\theta_n-\theta_n\). Since \(\widehat S_{-k,n}(O_{i,n})-\theta_n=\psi_n(O_{i,n})+\delta_{k,n}(O_{i,n})\), the centering identity yields
\[
\widehat\sigma_n^2=\sum_k w_{k,n}\mathbb P_{k,n}(\psi_n+\delta_{k,n})^2-e_n^2. \tag{3}
\]
Conditional Markov's inequality and the score rate give
\[
\sum_k w_{k,n}\mathbb P_{k,n}\delta_{k,n}^2=O_{P_n}(r_{S,n}^2). \tag{4}
\]
The common envelope from \(\texttt{lem:uniform-canonical-gradient-bound}\) gives
\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_n(O_{i,n})^2-\sigma_n^2=O_{P_n}(n^{-1/2}), \tag{5}
\]
and Cauchy--Schwarz with (4) gives
\[
\left|\sum_k w_{k,n}\mathbb P_{k,n}(\psi_n\delta_{k,n})\right|=O_{P_n}(r_{S,n}). \tag{6}
\]
Because \(r_{\pi,n},r_{q,n}\to0\), eventually \(r_{q,n}^2+r_{\pi,n}r_{q,n}\lesssim r_{\pi,n}+2r_{q,n}=r_{S,n}\). The estimator expansion and bounded variance of \(\psi_n\) consequently give
\[
e_n=O_{P_n}(r_{S,n}+n^{-1/2}),\qquad e_n^2=O_{P_n}(r_{S,n}+n^{-1/2}). \tag{7}
\]
Expanding (3) and applying (4)--(7) proves
\[
\widehat\sigma_n^2-\sigma_n^2=O_{P_n}(r_{S,n}+n^{-1/2})
\]
uniformly over \(\mathbf P\in\mathscr C\).

Apply \(\texttt{lem:uniform-bounded-triangular-clt}\) to \(Z_{i,n}=\psi_n(O_{i,n})\), \(v_n=\sigma_n\), the common envelope \(M\), and \(v_\star=\sigma_\star\). Thus
\[
\sup_{\mathbf P\in\mathscr C}\sup_t\left|P_n\!\left(\frac1{\sigma_n\sqrt n}\sum_i\psi_n(O_{i,n})\le t\right)-\Phi(t)\right|\to0.
\]
Variance consistency and \(\sigma_n\ge\sigma_\star\) give
\[
\left|\frac{\widehat\sigma_n}{\sigma_n}-1\right|=\frac{|\widehat\sigma_n^2-\sigma_n^2|}{\sigma_n(\widehat\sigma_n+\sigma_n)}\le\frac{|\widehat\sigma_n^2-\sigma_n^2|}{\sigma_\star^2}=o_{P_n}(1)
\]
uniformly; hence \(P_n(\widehat\sigma_n\le\sigma_\star/2)\to0\) uniformly. Put
\[
Z_n=\frac1{\sigma_n\sqrt n}\sum_i\psi_n(O_{i,n}),\qquad a_n=\frac{\widehat\sigma_n}{\sigma_n},\qquad b_n=\frac{\sqrt nR_n}{\sigma_n}.
\]
On the positive-denominator event the studentized statistic is \((Z_n+b_n)/a_n\), with \(a_n-1=o_{P_n}(1)\) and \(b_n=o_{P_n}(1)\) uniformly. For fixed \(0<\delta<1/2\), on \(\{|a_n-1|\le\delta,|b_n|\le\delta\}\), its distribution function is squeezed between distribution functions of \(Z_n\) at arguments differing from the target by at most \(\delta(1+|t|)\). On compact \(t\)-sets, uniform continuity of \(\Phi\) and the oracle Kolmogorov bound control the squeeze. Outside a sufficiently large compact set, the same bound and the normal tails control both distribution functions. Letting first \(n\to\infty\) and then \(\delta\downarrow0\) proves uniform Kolmogorov convergence. The zero-denominator convention affects only an event of uniformly vanishing probability.

Finally, on the positive-denominator event,
\[
\left\{\theta_n\in[\widehat\theta_n\mathbin\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\widehat\sigma_n/\sqrt n]\right\}=\left\{\left|\frac{\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_n)}{\widehat\sigma_n}\right|\le z_{1-\alpha/2}\right\}.
\]
The uniform limit at the two critical values and continuity of \(\Phi\) give coverage \(1-\alpha\).

Normalize \(X_{i,n}=Z_{i,n}/v_n\). Then \(E[X_{i,n}]=0\), \(E[X_{i,n}^2]=1\), and \(|X_{i,n}|\le B:=M/v_\star\). Let \(G_1,\ldots,G_n\) be independent standard normal variables. For any \(f\in C^3(\mathbb R)\) with bounded third derivative, replace the summands in \(n^{-1/2}\sum_iX_{i,n}\) one at a time by \(n^{-1/2}G_i\). Taylor expansion about the sum of the unreplaced terms has identical constant, linear, and quadratic expectations because the paired summands have the same first two moments. The third-order remainder gives
\[\left|E f\!\left(n^{-1/2}\sum_iX_{i,n}\right)-Ef(G_1)\right|\le\frac{C_B}{\sqrt n}\lVert f^{(3)}\rVert_\infty,\]
where \(C_B\) is common because \(E|X_{i,n}|^3\le B\). Fix a nondecreasing \(C^3\) cutoff that is zero on \(( -\infty,0]\), one on \([1,\infty)\), and has bounded third derivative. Its upper and lower \(\eta\)-smoothings of \(1\{z\le t\}\) have third derivatives bounded by \(C\eta^{-3}\). Hence, uniformly in \(t\) and the row law,
\[\Phi(t-\eta)-C_Bn^{-1/2}\eta^{-3}\le P\!\left(n^{-1/2}\sum_iX_{i,n}\le t\right)\le\Phi(t+\eta)+C_Bn^{-1/2}\eta^{-3}.\]
Since \(\sup_t|\Phi(t+\eta)-\Phi(t)|\le\eta/\sqrt{2\pi}\), choosing \(\eta=n^{-1/8}\) proves the asserted uniform Kolmogorov convergence.

The equivalence \(\sigma_n^2=0\Longleftrightarrow Q_{0,P_n}=Q_{1,P_n}\), the identities \(\theta_n=0\) and \(\psi_n=0\) at equality, the failure of the oracle first-order Gaussian pivot, and the weighted-Neumann second variation all follow from \(\texttt{lem:equality-degeneracy-and-second-variation}\). Thus equality is exactly the degeneracy boundary; it is not merely one sufficient example of degeneracy.

For a centered Gaussian quadratic calibration with Hessian eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\), \(\texttt{lem:gaussian-quadratic-spectral-criterion}\) proves
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\lambda_j(Z_j^2-1)\text{ exists in }L^2
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\lambda_j^2<\infty. \tag{1}
\]
For a collection of laws, approximation by a common finite spectral truncation is uniformly valid in mean square exactly when
\[
\lim_{J\to\infty}\sup_P\sum_{j>J}\lambda_j(P)^2=0. \tag{2}
\]
Hence a Hilbert--Schmidt Hessian and the uniform tail condition (2) are necessary for the proposed unregularized centered spectral calibration, and they are sufficient for the corresponding Gaussian quadratic limit objects to be well defined and uniformly approximable by finite-rank truncations. Further estimator and resampling consistency would still have to be proved separately.

The frozen model does not guarantee even the necessary compactness. At the admissible equality law constructed in \(\texttt{lem:conditional-hessian-spectral-obstruction}\), there is an infinite-dimensional closed observed-score subspace \(\mathcal E\) such that the compression of every Riesz representative \(H^\circ\) of the second derivative obeys
\[
\Pi_{\mathcal E}H^\circ\vert_{\mathcal E}=\lambda_\circ I_{\mathcal E},\qquad \lambda_\circ>0. \tag{3}
\]
The identity on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is not compact, so (3) rules out compactness and therefore rules out the Hilbert--Schmidt property. On the \(J\)-dimensional Gaussian subexperiment spanned by any \(J\) orthonormal vectors in \(\mathcal E\), the quadratic form is
\[
\lambda_\circ\sum_{j=1}^J(Z_j^2-1).
\]
Its characteristic-function modulus tends to zero at every nonzero argument as \(J\to\infty\), by \(\texttt{lem:gaussian-quadratic-spectral-criterion}\), so these restricted quadratic laws have no tight unregularized limit. This counterexample is a member-law obstruction, so a theorem asserted uniformly over the full frozen parent class cannot assume it away. Covariate smoothing, a finite-rank restriction, or another explicit regularization is therefore mathematically necessary before a spectral equality calibration can be formulated.

Finally, \(\texttt{lem:vanishing-variance-studentization}\) proves that the regular first-order conclusion does extend beyond fixed variance separation whenever the estimator remainder is \(o_P(\sigma_n/\sqrt n)\), the variance error is \(o_P(\sigma_n^2)\), and \(\sqrt n\,\sigma_n\to\infty\), uniformly over the sequence class under consideration. It also gives the corresponding uniform Wald coverage. These conclusions establish the claimed positive transition regime and the claimed negative result for the unregularized full-class equality route. They do not exclude a slower, regularized, non-spectral confidence construction, as stated.

Suppress the row index. First suppose \(Q_0(\cdot\mid x)=Q_1(\cdot\mid x)=Q(\cdot\mid x)\) almost surely. The diagonal coupling has zero cost, so \(V(x)=0\) and \(\theta=0\). Let \((u_0,u_1)\) be any continuous mutually conjugate optimal dual pair. The diagonal coupling is optimal, and complementary slackness gives
\[
u_0(x,y)+u_1(x,y)=0
\]
for \(Q(\cdot\mid x)\)-almost every \(y\). The density is bounded below and quadratic conjugate potentials are continuous, so the identity holds for every \(y\in\mathcal Y\). Dual feasibility therefore gives, for every \(y,z\in\mathcal Y\),
\[
u_1(x,z)-u_1(x,y)\le\lVert z-y\rVert_2^2,\qquad
u_1(x,y)-u_1(x,z)\le\lVert z-y\rVert_2^2. \tag{1}
\]
The uniformly convex set \(\mathcal Y\) is convex. Partition the segment from \(y\) to \(z\) into \(m\) equal pieces and sum (1) along the pieces. This yields
\[
|u_1(x,z)-u_1(x,y)|\le m\left(\frac{\lVert z-y\rVert_2}{m}\right)^2
=\frac{\lVert z-y\rVert_2^2}{m}.
\]
Letting \(m\to\infty\) shows that \(u_1(x,\cdot)\), and hence \(u_0(x,\cdot)\), is constant. The centered potentials vanish. Thus \(\psi=V-\theta=0\), and \(\sigma^2=0\).

Conversely, if \(\sigma^2=E[\psi^2]=0\), then \(\psi=0\) almost surely. Conditional on \(X=x,A=a\), fixed overlap gives
\[
V(x)-\theta+\frac{\phi_a(x,Y)}{\pi_a(x)}=0
\quad Q_a(\cdot\mid x)\text{-almost surely}. \tag{2}
\]
Integrating (2) with respect to \(Q_a(\cdot\mid x)\) and using \(\int\phi_a\,dQ_a=0\) gives \(V(x)=\theta\). Substitution into (2) gives \(\phi_a(x,\cdot)=0\) almost surely. Positivity of \(q_a\) and continuity of a quadratic conjugate potential make each \(u_a(x,\cdot)\) constant. The sum of these two constants equals the dual value \(V(x)\), whereas dual feasibility evaluated at \(y_0=y_1\) makes the sum nonpositive. Since \(V(x)=W_2^2(Q_0,Q_1)\ge0\), one has \(V(x)=0\). The Wasserstein metric separates probability laws on compact \(\mathcal Y\), so \(Q_0(\cdot\mid x)=Q_1(\cdot\mid x)\). It also follows that \(\theta=0\). This proves the equivalence. At equality the oracle quotient, under the frozen zero-denominator convention, is identically zero. Its distribution function is \(1\{t\ge0\}\), and
\[
\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}|1\{t\ge0\}-\Phi(t)|=\frac12. \tag{3}
\]

It remains to calculate the local second variation. Put \(\delta_x=h_1(x,\cdot)-h_0(x,\cdot)\), and, for \(r\in[0,1]\), define
\[
\rho_{r,t}=q+t\{(1-r)h_0+rh_1\},\qquad j_{r,t}=tq\nabla_yw_x.
\]
The weighted Neumann equation gives \(\partial_r\rho_{r,t}+\nabla_y\cdot j_{r,t}=0\) and zero normal flux. Since \(\rho_{r,t}\) stays bounded away from zero, the velocity \(v_{r,t}=j_{r,t}/\rho_{r,t}\) is uniformly Lipschitz in \(y\) under the displayed smoothness hypotheses. Let \(F_{r,t}\) be its flow starting from the identity. Differentiating \(\int f(F_{r,t}(y))q_{0,t}(y)d\ell_{\mathcal Y}(y)\) in \(r\), and using the continuity equation and zero flux, shows that \((F_{r,t})_\#(q_{0,t}d\ell_{\mathcal Y})=\rho_{r,t}d\ell_{\mathcal Y}\). Hence \((\operatorname{id},F_{1,t})_\#(q_{0,t}d\ell_{\mathcal Y})\) is a coupling of the two endpoints. Along each flow line, Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
\lVert F_{1,t}(y)-y\rVert_2^2\le\int_0^1\lVert v_{r,t}(F_{r,t}(y))\rVert_2^2dr.
\]
Integration over the initial law and the pushforward identity therefore yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
W_2^2(q_{0,t}d\ell_{\mathcal Y},q_{1,t}d\ell_{\mathcal Y})
&\le\int_0^1\!\int_{\mathcal Y}\frac{\lVert j_{r,t}\rVert_2^2}{\rho_{r,t}}d\ell_{\mathcal Y}dr\\
&=t^2E_x+O(|t|^3),
\end{aligned} \tag{4}
\]
where \(E_x=\int q(x,y)\lVert\nabla_yw_x(y)\rVert_2^2d\ell_{\mathcal Y}(y)\). The remainder in (4) is uniform in \(x\), because \(q\ge c\) and the displayed path functions are uniformly bounded.

For the reverse inequality, let \(\gamma_{x,t}\) be an optimal coupling and write \(W_{x,t}^2=\int\lVert y_1-y_0\rVert_2^2d\gamma_{x,t}\). The weak Neumann identity and the two marginal constraints imply
\[
tE_x=\int\{w_x(y_1)-w_x(y_0)\}d\gamma_{x,t}(y_0,y_1). \tag{5}
\]
Taylor's formula along the segment in convex \(\mathcal Y\), followed by Cauchy--Schwarz, gives
\[
|t|E_x\le\{E_x+O(|t|)\}^{1/2}W_{x,t}
+\frac12\lVert\nabla_y^2w_x\rVert_\infty W_{x,t}^2. \tag{6}
\]
The upper bound (4) gives \(W_{x,t}=O(|t|)\). If \(E_x>0\), divide (6) by \(|t|\) and take a lower limit to obtain \(\liminf_{t\to0}W_{x,t}^2/t^2\ge E_x\). If \(E_x=0\), positivity of \(q\) gives \(\nabla w_x=0\), the Neumann equation gives \(\delta_x=0\), and the same conclusion is immediate. Together with (4),
\[
W_{x,t}^2=t^2E_x+o(t^2). \tag{7}
\]
Finally, (4) divided by \(t^2\) supplies a common integrable bound, while (7) gives pointwise convergence. Dominated convergence over \(P_X\) yields
\[
\theta(P_t)=t^2\int E_xdP_X(x)+o(t^2)=t^2\mathcal E+o(t^2).
\]
The first derivative is zero by equality, so the second directional derivative is \(2\mathcal E\), as claimed.

Put \(S_J=\sum_{j=1}^J\lambda_j(Z_j^2-1)\).  Independence, centering, and \(E[(Z_j^2-1)^2]=2\) give, whenever \(J>L\),
\[
E[(S_J-S_L)^2]=2\sum_{j=L+1}^J\lambda_j^2. \tag{1}
\]
Thus \((S_J)\) is Cauchy in \(L^2\) if and only if \(\sum_j\lambda_j^2<\infty\), which proves the first assertion by completeness of \(L^2\).  The same identity uniformly over \(\lambda\in\Lambda\) gives
\[
\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}E\!\left[\left\{\sum_{j>J}\lambda_j(Z_j^2-1)\right\}^2\right]
=2\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\sum_{j>J}\lambda_j^2,
\]
and proves the common-truncation criterion in both directions.

If \(\lambda_j\ge0\), the uncentered partial sums increase almost surely and
\[
E\!\left[\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jZ_j^2\right]=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j. \tag{2}
\]
When the right side is finite, the expected nonnegative tail tends to zero, so the partial sums converge in \(L^1\).  Conversely, \(L^1\) convergence bounds their expectations, and (2) forces \(\sum_j\lambda_j<\infty\).

For the last assertion, the characteristic function of the actual full centered partial sum is
\[
\varphi_{S_J}(t)=\prod_{j\le J}e^{-it\lambda_j}(1-2it\lambda_j)^{-1/2},
\qquad
|\varphi_{S_J}(t)|=\prod_{j\le J}(1+4t^2\lambda_j^2)^{-1/4}. \tag{3}
\]
Let \(m_J=|\{j\le J:\lambda_j=\lambda_\circ\}|\).  By hypothesis \(m_J\to\infty\), and every factor in (3) is at most one.  Hence, for every \(t\ne0\),
\[
|\varphi_{S_J}(t)|
\le(1+4t^2\lambda_\circ^2)^{-m_J/4}\longrightarrow0. \tag{4}
\]
Suppose some full-partial-sum subsequence \(S_{J_r}\) converged weakly to a real random variable \(S\).  Since \(x\mapsto e^{itx}\) is bounded and continuous, weak convergence would give \(\varphi_{S_{J_r}}(t)\to E[e^{itS}]\) for every \(t\).  Equation (4) would therefore imply \(E[e^{itS}]=0\) for every \(t\ne0\).  But dominated convergence gives \(E[e^{itS}]\to1\) as \(t\to0\), a contradiction.  Thus the actual full partial sums have no weakly convergent subsequence.

Choose a nonconstant \(w\in C_c^\infty(\operatorname{int}\mathcal Y)\), and put
\[
g(y)=-q^\circ\Delta w(y),\qquad
\kappa=q^\circ\int_{\mathcal Y}\lVert\nabla w(y)\rVert_2^2d\ell_{\mathcal Y}(y)>0. \tag{1}
\]
Because \(w\) is compactly supported in the interior, \(\int g\,d\ell_{\mathcal Y}=0\) and the zero-flux boundary condition holds. For every bounded smooth function \(e\) on \(\mathcal X\), perturb only arm one by
\[
q_{0,t}=q^\circ,\qquad q_{1,t}(x,y)=q^\circ+t e(x)g(y). \tag{2}
\]
The strict interior condition in the lemma ensures that, for each fixed \(e\), (2) remains inside the density bounds and H\"older ball for all sufficiently small \(|t|\). Its observed-data score is
\[
s_e(x,a,y)=1\{a=1\}\frac{e(x)g(y)}{q^\circ}. \tag{3}
\]
For two such functions \(e,f\),
\[
\langle s_e,s_f\rangle_{L^2(P^\circ)}
=c_g\langle e,f\rangle_{L^2(P_X^\circ)},\qquad
c_g=\frac12\int_{\mathcal Y}\frac{g(y)^2}{q^\circ}d\ell_{\mathcal Y}(y)>0. \tag{4}
\]

The weighted Neumann solution for direction \(e(x)g(y)\) is \(w_e(x,y)=e(x)w(y)\). Applying \(\texttt{lem:equality-degeneracy-and-second-variation}\) and polarizing its quadratic energy gives the Hessian bilinear form
\[
D^2\theta_{P^\circ}[s_e,s_f]
=2\kappa\langle e,f\rangle_{L^2(P_X^\circ)}. \tag{5}
\]
Combining (4) and (5), and defining \(\lambda_\circ=2\kappa/c_g\), gives
\[
D^2\theta_{P^\circ}[s_e,s_f]
=\lambda_\circ\langle s_e,s_f\rangle_{L^2(P^\circ)}. \tag{6}
\]

For completeness, the full outcome-score Hessian is a bounded bilinear form. If \(d(x,\cdot)\) is the difference of the two conditional-density path derivatives and \(v_x\) solves \(-q^\circ\Delta v_x=d(x,\cdot)\) with zero flux and mean zero, integration by parts and the Poincar\'e inequality give
\[
q^\circ\lVert\nabla v_x\rVert_2^2
=\int_{\mathcal Y}d(x,y)v_x(y)d\ell_{\mathcal Y}(y)
\le C_{\mathcal Y}\lVert d(x,\cdot)\rVert_2\lVert\nabla v_x\rVert_2.
\]
Thus the Neumann energy is bounded by a constant times \(\lVert d(x,\cdot)\rVert_2^2\). Fixed overlap and the bounds on \(q^\circ\) control this norm by the squared \(L^2(P^\circ)\)-norm of the observed outcome score. Polarization therefore gives a bounded symmetric bilinear form, and the Hilbert-space Riesz construction supplies a bounded self-adjoint representative \(H^\circ\).

Because \(P_X^\circ\) is nonatomic, \(L^2(P_X^\circ)\) is infinite dimensional. Bounded smooth functions are dense in this space: continuous functions are dense for a finite Borel measure on compact \(\mathcal X\), and continuous functions can be uniformly approximated on the closure of a Lipschitz domain by smooth functions. Hence the closure \(\mathcal E=\overline{\{s_e:e\text{ bounded and smooth}\}}\) is an infinite-dimensional closed subspace. Equation (6) extends to all of \(\mathcal E\) by continuity. If \(\Pi_{\mathcal E}\) is the orthogonal projection, then
\[
\Pi_{\mathcal E}H^\circ\vert_{\mathcal E}=\lambda_\circ I_{\mathcal E}. \tag{7}
\]
If \(H^\circ\) were compact, the left side of (7), as a composition of bounded maps with a compact map, would be compact. The right side is not compact: for any orthonormal sequence \(v_j\in\mathcal E\), the images \(\lambda_\circ v_j\) have no convergent subsequence. This contradiction proves noncompactness. Every Hilbert--Schmidt operator is compact, so \(H^\circ\) is not Hilbert--Schmidt. The compression therefore precludes any square-summable unregularized spectral representation.

Write
\[
Z_n=\frac1{\sigma_n\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_n(O_{i,n}).
\]
For fixed \(t\), Taylor's formula for the complex exponential, \(E[\psi_n]=0\), and \(E[\psi_n^2]=\sigma_n^2\) give
\[
E\exp\left(\frac{it\psi_n}{\sigma_n\sqrt n}\right)
=1-\frac{t^2}{2n}+\rho_n(t),
\]
where
\[
|\rho_n(t)|\le\frac{|t|^3E|\psi_n|^3}{6\sigma_n^3n^{3/2}}
\le\frac{|t|^3M_\psi}{6\sigma_n n^{3/2}}. \tag{1}
\]
The second inequality uses \(|\psi_n|^3\le M_\psi\psi_n^2\). Since \(\sqrt n\,\sigma_n\to\infty\), multiplying the last bound in (1) by \(n\) gives a quantity tending uniformly to zero. Independence within rows therefore yields
\[
E[e^{itZ_n}]
=\left\{1-\frac{t^2}{2n}+\rho_n(t)\right\}^n
\longrightarrow e^{-t^2/2}. \tag{2}
\]
The convergence is uniform over the stated collection. A subsequence argument turns (2) into uniform Kolmogorov convergence: if uniform convergence of distribution functions failed, choose a violating sequence of laws; (2) along that sequence gives weak convergence to the continuous standard-normal distribution, which implies convergence in Kolmogorov distance, a contradiction. Thus
\[
\sup_P\sup_t|P_n(Z_n\le t)-\Phi(t)|\to0. \tag{3}
\]

The variance condition and positivity of \(\sigma_n\) give
\[
\left|\frac{\widehat\sigma_n}{\sigma_n}-1\right|
=\frac{|\widehat\sigma_n^2-\sigma_n^2|}{\sigma_n(\widehat\sigma_n+\sigma_n)}
\le\frac{|\widehat\sigma_n^2-\sigma_n^2|}{\sigma_n^2}
=o_{P_n}(1) \tag{4}
\]
uniformly. In particular, \(P_n(\widehat\sigma_n>0)\to1\) uniformly. If \(R_n\) denotes the estimator remainder, the first relative-rate condition gives
\[
\frac{\sqrt nR_n}{\sigma_n}=o_{P_n}(1). \tag{5}
\]
On the event of a positive denominator, the studentized statistic equals
\[
\frac{Z_n+\sqrt nR_n/\sigma_n}{\widehat\sigma_n/\sigma_n}.
\]
Equations (3)--(5), using the same subsequence argument for uniformity, prove the asserted uniform standard-normal limit. The frozen zero-denominator convention changes the statistic only on an event of uniformly vanishing probability. Evaluating the limit at \(\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\) gives
\[
P_n\!\left(\theta_n\in\left[\widehat\theta_n\mathbin\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\widehat\sigma_n/\sqrt n\right]\right)\to1-\alpha
\]
uniformly. If the stated one-step remainder and variance bounds hold, the final assertion follows by substituting their deterministic upper envelopes into the two relative-rate conditions.
